Note::TexAccessor::vector_norm¶

Back to Note TeX Accessor API Reference

Signature¶

Note Note::TexAccessor::vector_norm() const

Rewrite Vector Notation To \vec{...}¶

vector_norm() rewrites every \mathbf{...}, \boldsymbol{...}, and \overrightarrow{...} call, and every bare \vec x (a single ASCII letter, space-separated, not yet braced), to the single canonical form \vec{...}. Use it before comparing or rendering TeX math source authored with mixed vector conventions, so \mathbf{v}, \vec v, and \vec{v} all collapse to one spelling.

\mathbf/\boldsymbol/\overrightarrow accept any brace-balanced content with no inner {/} (so \mathbf{AB}, not just single letters); the bare \vec x form only matches a single letter with no braces, since a multi-character bare form (\vec AB) is not valid TeX to begin with. An already-braced \vec{x} is left untouched — it is already canonical, and there is no third pass to normalize it further.

The rewrite is lexical and single-pass: it does not recurse into nested braces, does not distinguish math mode from text mode, and treats \mathbf{} (empty content) as a non-match, left unchanged. Other bold or arrow commands (\mathbb, \Vec, \overleftarrow) are not recognized and pass through untouched — only the three named commands above are rewritten.

The operation is shape-preserving, cell-independent, and returns a fresh Note. Undefined input remains undefined; Bool, Int64, Float64, and Bytes receivers are rejected because TeX source is Text.

Example 1: All Three Long Forms And The Bare Form¶

std::cout << pluss::make_note(
    {"\\mathbf{v} + \\boldsymbol{w} - \\overrightarrow{AB}"})
    .tex().vector_norm()
    << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["\\vec{v} + \\vec{w} - \\vec{AB}"]

Example 2: A Bare Form Next To An Already-Braced Form¶

std::cout << pluss::make_note({"\\vec v + \\vec{u}"}).tex().vector_norm()
          << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["\\vec{v} + \\vec{u}"]

Both cells read \vec{v} + \vec{u} after the call; the second term was already canonical and is copied through unchanged.

Example 3: Non-Matches Are Left Alone¶

std::cout << pluss::make_note({"plain text \\mathbf{}"}).tex().vector_norm()
          << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["plain text \\mathbf{}"]

An empty \mathbf{} group has no content to capture, so it is not a match.

Example 4: A 2-D Grid, Shape Preserved¶

const auto grid = pluss::make_note(
    std::vector<std::string>{"\\mathbf{a}", "plain", "\\vec b", ""},
    std::array<std::int64_t, 2>{2, 2});
std::cout << grid.tex().vector_norm() << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[2, 2], dim=2, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
[
  ["\\vec{a}", "plain"], 
  ["\\vec{b}", ""]
]

Example 5: Undefined And Non-Text Input¶

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << pluss::Note::undefined().tex().vector_norm().defined()
          << '\n';
try {
  (void)pluss::note::make(std::vector<std::int64_t>{1, 2}).tex().vector_norm();
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "Int64: rejected\n";
}

Output¶

false
Int64: rejected
